direct_answer:
Petrom (OMV Petrom) conducted its Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) in 2023 (reviewed in 2024) as a five-step ESRS-based process covering all fully consolidated entities where it is operator and/or holds >50% with controlling influence, and including each value-chain segment (upstream, own operations, downstream) [Source 2][Source 3]. The five steps were: (1) build a long list of ESRS topics plus other guideline topics and shortlist them based on relevance to OMV Petrom’s activities, business relationships and geographies; (2) interview internal subject matter experts to identify/formulate impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs); (3) engage stakeholders—ten internal/external stakeholder groups (employees, customers, suppliers/contractors/business partners, capital market participants, NGOs, authorities, communities, associations/networks, media, education/science/research)—to identify topics of highest relevance and to validate/inform internal assessments; (4) assess and score IROs in workshops to determine impact and financial materiality; and (5) prioritise topics using predefined thresholds [Source 2].

For impact materiality, impacts were assessed across own operations and business relationships using criteria of scale, scope, irremediability and likelihood (for potential impacts), considering predominant positive/negative impacts and various time horizons; thresholds applied were 8 for environmental topics and 5 for social and governance topics [Source 4]. For financial materiality, risks/opportunities were scored by magnitude of financial effect (0–3) and likelihood (0–5), with a financial materiality threshold of 1.5 [Source 1]. The process used internal reports/operational data, ESG reporting and workshops, reviewed sector/industry standards (e.g., GRI, SASB) and included external and internal stakeholders [Source 3]. Governance-wise, the Corporate Sustainability sub-department coordinated the DMA; internal experts provided topic inputs; senior management provided consultation; and the Executive Board approved the final material topics/subtopics in Dec 2023 [Source 1].

Material sustainability matters identified (i.e., the company’s “material topics” per its DMA mapping) were: climate change mitigation; energy; pollution of air; pollution of soil; water; direct impact drivers of biodiversity loss; process safety; own workforce—working conditions and training/skills/development; workers in the value chain—working conditions and other work-related rights; and affected communities—communities’ economic, social and cultural rights [Source 6].

However, the retrieved passages do not explicitly state which of these matters are material from both an impact and a financial perspective (i.e., “double material” in the sense of meeting both impact and financial materiality criteria). The passages describe the DMA method and list material topics, but they do not provide a topic-by-topic split showing impact materiality vs financial materiality outcomes, nor identify which topics meet both dimensions [Source 1][Source 4][Source 6].
compliance_rationale: The evidence clearly describes the DMA process steps, stakeholder engagement, value-chain coverage, scoring criteria and thresholds for impact and financial materiality, and governance/approval of results [Source 1][Source 2][Source 3][Source 4]. It also provides a list of material topics resulting from the DMA [Source 6]. But it does not disclose which sustainability matters are material from both an impact and a financial perspective specifically, as requested (no explicit double-material list or per-topic impact vs financial determination) [Source 1][Source 6].
disclosure_gaps: Explicit identification of which sustainability matters are material from both impact and financial perspectives (a double-material subset), supported by the DMA results.

Topic-by-topic (or subtopic-by-subtopic) presentation of impact materiality scores/threshold outcomes vs financial materiality scores/threshold outcomes to evidence why each topic is impact-material, financial-material, or both.

Clear disclosure of interdependencies between impact and financial materiality outcomes (e.g., whether the assessment generally started from impacts and how impacts informed financial risks/opportunities) beyond general statements of criteria and thresholds.
key_findings: DMA followed a five-step ESRS-based process: long list/shortlist topics; internal expert interviews; stakeholder engagement across ten stakeholder groups; scoring in workshops; prioritisation using thresholds [Source 2].
Impact materiality criteria used: scale, scope, irremediability, and likelihood (for potential impacts); thresholds: 8 (environment) and 5 (social/governance) [Source 4].
Financial materiality criteria used: magnitude of financial effect (0–3) and likelihood (0–5); financial materiality threshold: 1.5 [Source 1].
Assessment boundary included fully consolidated entities under OMV Petrom’s control and included upstream, own operations, and downstream value chain segments [Source 2][Source 3].

Stakeholder engagement included employees, customers, suppliers/contractors/business partners, capital market participants, NGOs, authorities, communities, associations/networks, media, and education/science/research; affected stakeholders were consulted to validate and inform internal assessments [Source 2][Source 4].

Material topics listed in the Sustainability Statement mapping include: climate change mitigation; energy; pollution of air/soil; water; direct impact drivers of biodiversity loss; process safety; own workforce (working conditions; training/skills/development); workers in the value chain (working conditions; other work-related rights); affected communities (economic, social and cultural rights) [Source 6].
The retrieved passages do not specify which of the listed material topics are material in both dimensions (impact and financial) [Source 1][Source 6].
